title: Why is an immutable value class (e.g. a Money with final fields where add() returns a NEW instance) inherently thread-safe and freely shareable across threads WITHOUT any synchronization, whereas a mutable equivalent needs synchronization on every read/write — and how is this the same principle behind String, Java records, and value-over-object functional style?
shortTitle: Why an immutable value class is inherently thread-safe

s1_definition.profdef: An immutable value class is inherently thread-safe because it has no mutable state, so there is nothing for concurrent threads to corrupt; once constructed, its fields never change, and the Java Memory Model guarantees that correctly constructed final fields are visible to all threads without synchronization. Any operation that would change the value, such as `add`, returns a new instance instead of mutating the existing one, so threads only ever share read-only objects. A mutable equivalent, by contrast, has fields that threads can write concurrently, creating race conditions, so every read and write must be synchronized to be correct. This same principle, immutability guaranteeing safe sharing, is why `String`, Java records, and the value-over-object functional style are all built on immutable data.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine a printed demand draft for a fixed amount. Any number of clerks can read that draft at the same time with no confusion, because nobody can change it; the number on it is permanent. That is an immutable Money object: many threads can read it simultaneously, safely, with no locks. Now imagine instead a shared chalkboard balance that any clerk can erase and rewrite. If two clerks write at the same time, you get a garbled number or a lost update, so the bank must install a single lock on the chalkboard and force clerks to take turns. That is a mutable object needing synchronization on every read and write. Immutability removes the chalkboard problem entirely by never allowing anyone to erase.
s1_definition.oneliner: Immutable objects are thread-safe because there is no mutable state to race on, so they share freely without locks, while mutable objects must synchronize every access.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An immutable value class is inherently thread-safe because it has no mutable state, so there is nothing for concurrent threads to corrupt; once constructed, its fields never change, and the Java Memory Model guarantees that correctly constructed final fields are visible to all threads without synchronization. Any operation that would change the value, such as `add`, returns a new instance instead of mutating the existing one, so threads only ever share read-only objects. A mutable equivalent, by contrast, has fields that threads can write concurrently, creating race conditions, so every read and write must be synchronized to be correct. This same principle, immutability guaranteeing safe sharing, is why `String`, Java records, and the value-over-object functional style are all built on immutable data.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine a printed demand draft for a fixed amount. Any number of clerks can read that draft at the same time with no confusion, because nobody can change it; the number on it is permanent. That is an immutable Money object: many threads can read it simultaneously, safely, with no locks. Now imagine instead a shared chalkboard balance that any clerk can erase and rewrite. If two clerks write at the same time, you get a garbled number or a lost update, so the bank must install a single lock on the chalkboard and force clerks to take turns. That is a mutable object needing synchronization on every read and write. Immutability removes the chalkboard problem entirely by never allowing anyone to erase.

**One line to remember:** Immutable objects are thread-safe because there is no mutable state to race on, so they share freely without locks, while mutable objects must synchronize every access.

sections.s2_technical:
Thread-safety problems come from shared mutable state. When two threads read and write the same field without coordination, you get race conditions: lost updates, torn reads, and visibility problems where one thread does not see another's write. The traditional fix is synchronization, which serializes access and establishes happens-before ordering so writes become visible, but synchronization adds contention and complexity.

An immutable value class sidesteps the entire problem. Because all fields are final and set once in the constructor, and there are no setters or mutating methods, the state can never change after construction. There is simply nothing to race on. Any operation that conceptually changes the value returns a new instance, so the original object is never modified. Two threads calling add on the same Money each get their own new Money, and the shared original is untouched.

There is a precise memory-model guarantee behind this. The Java Memory Model specifies that if an object is properly constructed, meaning the constructor does not let the this reference escape, then its final fields are guaranteed to be visible to any thread that sees the object, without any synchronization. This is called safe publication of final fields. So not only is there no mutation, but the initial values are guaranteed visible to all threads.

This is exactly why String is immutable: strings are shared constantly across threads and used as keys and cached, and immutability makes all of that safe and lock-free. Java records, from Java 16, are shallowly immutable data carriers with final fields, giving the same guarantee for simple value types. The value-over-object functional style, favored in modern Java and in functional languages, treats data as immutable values that are transformed into new values rather than mutated in place, which makes concurrent and parallel code far easier to reason about. A senior nuance is that immutable objects enable lock-free designs, safe caching, and use in concurrent collections as keys, and they pair naturally with atomic reference swaps for the rare case where you need a mutable holder of an immutable value. Another nuance is that immutability can create more short-lived objects, but modern garbage collectors handle short-lived allocations very efficiently, so the clarity and safety usually outweigh the allocation cost.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank runs many threads that read and combine Money values concurrently during end-of-day aggregation. With immutable Money, all those threads share the same objects with no locks and never corrupt anything. This is exactly why immutable value classes are inherently thread-safe.

Problem 2 — An older mutable balance holder let two threads update the same balance at once, and updates were lost. This is exactly the race condition that forces synchronization on every read and write.

Problem 3 — The demo runs many threads adding to a shared immutable Money and to a shared mutable counter, showing the immutable path is correct and lock-free while the unsynchronized mutable path loses updates. This is exactly the contrast.

The code has an immutable `Money`, a mutable `UnsafeBalance`, and a `ThreadSafeImmutableDemo` main class that launches concurrent tasks against both.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/concurrent/ThreadSafeImmutableDemo.java

# Run (immutable total is always correct; unsafe total varies and is usually lower)
java -cp out com.bank.concurrent.ThreadSafeImmutableDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: 8 threads, each adding 1 one thousand times, so the expected total is 8000.

Step 1: A shared immutable Money starts at zero, held inside an AtomicReference. A shared mutable UnsafeBalance also starts at zero.

Step 2: Eight threads start concurrently. Each thread loops a thousand times.

Step 3: For the immutable path, each iteration computes a new Money that is one larger and atomically swaps it into the reference. Because Money never changes, there is no corruption; the atomic reference ensures each swap sees the latest value and retries if needed, giving a correct lock-free accumulation.

Step 4: For the mutable path, each iteration reads the current int, adds one, and writes it back, with no synchronization. When two threads read the same value and both write back, one update is lost.

Step 5: After all threads finish, the immutable Money total equals exactly 8000, correct, achieved without any locks on the Money object itself because the object was never mutated.

Step 6: The unsafe mutable total is usually less than 8000 because of lost updates, demonstrating that a mutable object needs synchronization to be correct, while the immutable value never needed it.

```text
INFO: Expected total = 8000
INFO: Immutable Money total = Rs.8000 (CORRECT, no locks)
WARNING: Unsafe mutable total = 7421 (likely < expected, lost updates)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  8 threads × 1000 adds

  ─── Immutable Money path ───
  Thread A ─┐
  Thread B ─┼─ each builds NEW Money(cur+1) ─► AtomicReference.updateAndGet (CAS)
  ...       │        (original Money never mutated — nothing to race on)
  Thread H ─┘
     ▼
  total = Rs.8000  ✓ CORRECT, lock-free

  ─── Mutable UnsafeBalance path ───
  Thread A: read 100 ─┐
  Thread B: read 100 ─┼─ both write 101  → one update LOST
     ▼
  total = 7421 (varies) ✗ needs synchronization
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Immutable vs Mutable Under Concurrency ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<final>> Money (immutable) │   │   UnsafeBalance (mutable)     │
  │ - final amount: BigDecimal    │   │ - value: int                  │
  │ + add(Money): Money (NEW)     │   │ + add(int): void (racy RMW)   │
  │ thread-safe: YES (no state    │   │ thread-safe: NO (needs sync   │
  │   to mutate; final published) │   │   on every read/write)        │
  └───────────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────────┘

  Memory-model guarantee:
    properly constructed final fields are visible to all threads
    WITHOUT synchronization (safe publication).

  Same principle elsewhere:
    String  → immutable → shared/cached/keys safely
    record  → final components → value carrier, same guarantee
    functional value-over-object → transform to NEW value, never mutate
  Rare mutable holder → AtomicReference<ImmutableValue> + CAS.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An immutable value class is inherently thread-safe because thread-safety problems come from shared mutable state, and an immutable object simply has none. All its fields are final and set once in the constructor, there are no setters, and any operation that would change the value, like add on a Money, returns a brand-new instance instead of modifying the existing one. So there is nothing for concurrent threads to corrupt. Two threads working with the same Money each produce their own new Money, and the shared original is never touched.

There is a precise guarantee from the Java Memory Model behind this. If an object is properly constructed, meaning its this reference does not escape during construction, then its final fields are guaranteed to be visible to any thread that sees the object, with no synchronization at all. That is called safe publication of final fields, and it means both that there is no mutation and that the initial values are reliably visible everywhere.

A mutable equivalent is the opposite. If a balance field can be written by multiple threads, then concurrent read-modify-write sequences race, and you get lost updates and visibility bugs. The only way to make it correct is to synchronize every read and every write, which adds locking, contention, and complexity. I demonstrated this with a simple counter: the immutable Money accumulation was always exactly correct and needed no locks on the Money object, while the unsynchronized mutable counter lost updates and ended up below the expected total.

This is the same principle behind several core parts of Java. String is immutable precisely because strings are shared, cached, and used as keys constantly, and immutability makes all of that safe and lock-free. Java records are shallowly immutable data carriers with final fields, giving the same guarantee for simple value types. And the value-over-object functional style treats data as immutable values transformed into new values rather than mutated in place, which is what makes concurrent and parallel code so much easier to reason about. In our banking aggregation, this lets many worker threads share immutable Money values with zero synchronization, and for the rare case where I need a mutable holder, I wrap an immutable value in an AtomicReference and swap it with a compare-and-set, keeping the whole design lock-free and correct.
